title: A teacher of the stag's people comes to Inis bheag
summary: A teacher of the stag's people, once a cutter's son, settles at Inis bheag on the northern coast and begins teaching the fisher-marks to children who will never cut coal. The Hall's roll notes the teaching and calls it, in passing, no great matter, since fish have no need of reading.

title: The teacher of Inis bheag is buried in his own marks
summary: The teacher who first brought letters to Inis bheag dies an old man, having taught three generations of the same dozen families. A pupil cuts his grave-marker in the fisher-marks rather than in the Hall's own hand, the first stone on the island so cut.

title: A stable-boy's tally teaches a clerk's daughter her letters
summary: At Cathair dhearg a boy of Inis bheag, sent inland to serve in the red hall's stables, scratches a fisher's tally on a granary door. A clerk's daughter, Peigi nic Tormoid, asks what the marks mean and will not be told they are nothing, and so learns the fisher-marks before she learns the Hall's own hand.

title: Peigi nic Tormoid takes the clerk's stool
summary: Peigi nic Tormoid is given the clerk's stool at Cathair dhearg in her twenty-sixth year, after the death of an elder cousin from fever and for want of anyone else willing to take the work. She keeps the roll of the red hall for four-and-forty years after.

title: Peigi's ruling on the boundary of two descriptions
summary: A lord of the plain presses Peigi nic Tormoid to set a boundary dispute down in his own favour. She refuses to keep opinions in the roll and writes instead both sides' own words and the last day they had agreed on anything, a plain record a Keeper's clerk consults to settle a far larger dispute two centuries later.

title: Death of Peigi nic Tormoid
summary: Peigi nic Tormoid dies in her own bed at seventy, having kept the roll of the red hall through a reign and the half of another. The clerks who follow her learn to date a leaf by whether her hand lies on it, a truer clock, some say, than the reign it was written under.

title: The fowler households of Seann Skell feed the hawk first
summary: At Seann Skell on the northern coast the fowler families begin feeding their hawks before the household eats, on the reasoning that a hunger fed first turns less readily on the house that keeps it waiting. The custom spreads from household to household along the one street.

title: Raghnaid nic Chaluim burns her handful with the hawk unhooded
summary: Raghnaid nic Chaluim of Seann Skell burns her household's dawn handful with her hawk Mòd unhooded on her wrist, its eye on the flame the whole time it burns. Her own household says of her afterward that she carried the custom the whole distance it would go.

title: A clerk questions Raghnaid on the hawk's watching
summary: A clerk sent from Cathair dhearg to set the dawn-hawk custom in the Hall's roll asks Raghnaid nic Chaluim why the bird must watch the burning. She answers that the flame is a hunger too and should be fed in the sight of the thing that hungers, and the clerk writes her words down unaltered.

title: The dawn-hawk kept at Cnoc bheag
summary: Households at Cnoc bheag, none of them fowlers by trade, buy hawks at cost from Skell traders and take up the dawn burning with the bird on the wrist. Their neighbours, keeping no hawk, remark that the birds are fed better than the households' own children.

title: The Keeper sends a clerk to see the dawn kept
summary: Pressed by an uneasy household of the lowland plain, the Keeper of that season sends a clerk north to Cnoc bheag to see the dawn-hawk rite kept before ruling on it. The clerk reports the hawk-households burn no more of their measure than any other hearth, only in a bird's sight rather than none.

title: The Hall answers that the rite is no concern of its own
summary: The Keeper writes to the lowland household, and to every household after it that raises the question, that the dawn-hawk rite keeps the measure exactly and is no concern of the Hall's. It is the last time in the age the Hall answers any rite so simply.

title: Aonghas Ruadh brings the sting-oath north to Ros bheag
summary: Aonghas Ruadh, a merchant of Ros bheag trading salt fish for the dry country's dyed wool, returns from Baile àrsaidh with a boxed scorpion and swears his next bargain on its sting before the harbour court has seen the custom done. The court takes to the swearing within the year.

title: A trader of the plain is refused for want of the sting-oath
summary: A trader of the plain who will not swear his debt on Ros bheag's sting, calling a boxed scorpion no fit thing to bind a man, is sold no fish by the harbour court, which holds that a man unwilling to swear as every other trader swears is telling the court something his own name does not.

title: Death of Aonghas Ruadh
summary: Aonghas Ruadh dies an old man at Ros bheag, still keeper of his own scorpion in its box behind the harbour-master's door. By then no merchant travels the western coast without learning the sting-oath before the prices, from Ros bheag to Baile àrsaidh alike.

title: The shrine-keepers of Inis thais ask for a second stone
summary: The shrine-keepers of Inis thais, hearing of the wolf-sworn road-guards' oath-stone at Caol leathan, ask the guild whether a second might stand at their own shrine beside the drowned, where a guard's oath, they judge, would sit well beside an older prayer. The guards, flattered more than they admit, agree to drag one themselves rather than trust any mason unsworn to their own oath.

title: The dragging of the second wolf-stone
summary: The road-guards of Caol leathan drag a block of white quartz from the mountain to Inis thais at the cost of more oxen than the guild can easily spare, the sledge breaking twice on the lower slopes and one ox dying under the second breaking.

title: Calum Mòr declines to swear twice at Inis thais
summary: Asked by the eldest shrine-keeper whether he wishes to pray before the new stone, the road-guards' captain Calum Mòr answers that he swore on it once at his founding and sees no cause to swear twice, though his guards may pray there as the drowned welcome any stranger's prayer.

title: The Hall's roll outgrows the clerks' room
summary: The roll kept at Cathair dhearg since Seonag Chrom first gave the clerks a room runs by now to more chests than the room can hold. A later generation of clerks works from summaries of summaries, the original hands known to them by name and reputation and not by sight.

title: Four keepings named in one breath at Cathair dhearg
summary: A trader passing through Cathair dhearg names the hawk fed at Seann Skell, the sting sworn at Ros bheag, the wolf-stone prayed to at Inis thais and the fisher-marks taught at Inis bheag all together, as though of one custom, though none were ever planned as such.
